contribution: The second unit of the French chapter: beginners learn to count from 0 to 100 (with the vigesimal 70–99 of France and the Belgian and Swiss forms), to read, say and catch prices in euros by ear, and to ask for a price or a repetition politely, in a market and café scenario on the ITER visit.
learn: count from 0 to 100 in French, including the tricky numbers from 70 to 99.
understand a price in euros when you hear it, and say and write prices the French way.
ask what something costs and ask the seller to repeat, slow down or write the price down.
prior: Greetings and polite *vous* (chapter *Bonjour ! Introducing yourself*)

activities.text: The morning before your visit to ITER, your group walks through the market in Aix-en-Provence, about 35 kilometres south of the site. You buy two lemons and a bag of apricots for the bus. The seller weighs them, smiles and tells you the price, fast. You hear four words, and the only one you recognise is *euros*. Behind you, other people are waiting.
activities.question: How can you find out what to pay, and how can you be sure that you heard it right?

activities.text:
Sentence starters

  • In Finnish, 23 is built from …
  • English and Finnish both put … first.
  • If I do not catch a price, I can …
  • A number that looks easy but could be hard is …, because …

activities.title: Think about it: how numbers are built
activities.prompt: Finnish says *kaksikymmentäkolme* (two-ten-three), Swedish *tjugotre*, English *twenty-three*. How are these numbers built? Older English also counted in twenties: *four score and seven* (Lincoln, 1863) was 87. Then think about the market: what can you do if you do not catch a price?
activities.pair: Discuss with a partner for three minutes, then write a few lines together.
activities.model: All three languages build 23 from the tens and then the units: *kaksikymmentä* + *kolme*, *tjugo* + *tre*, *twenty* + *three*. *Four score and seven* is $4 \cdot 20 + 7$ = 87, so it multiplies and then adds. If we do not catch a price, we can look at the scales or the till, hold out a bigger note, ask the seller to repeat it or to write it down, or show our phone's calculator.
criteria: We say that the tens come first and the units after them.
We explain *four score and seven* as a calculation ($4 \cdot 20 + 7$).
We name at least two ways to understand a price we did not catch.

activities.title: Prediction 1: seventy
activities.prompt: In French, 60 is *soixante* and 10 is *dix*. How do you think a French person in France says 70? Commit now; the theory summary will show you.

choices.feedback: Right: in France 70 is 60 + 10, soixante-dix, and 71 is soixante et onze ($60 + 11$). French counts on from 60 with the numbers 10–19.
A good guess, and correct in Belgium and Switzerland, where 70 is septante. In France you will hear soixante-dix ($60 + 10$).
This would be 7 · 10, as in Finnish *seitsemänkymmentä*, but French does not build 70 like that. In France it is $60 + 10$: soixante-dix.
This is $60 + 7 = 67$. Seventy is $60 + 10$: soixante-dix.

activities.title: Prediction 2: a price
activities.prompt: A café menu says 2,50 € for a croissant and a coffee. How does the waiter say this price? Commit now; the theory summary will show you.

choices.feedback: Right: the euros first, then the word *euros*, then the centimes without a word after them: deux euros cinquante.
This is 250 €, a hundred times more. The comma in 2,50 € is the French decimal comma: two euros and fifty centimes, deux euros cinquante.
This is 25 €. The comma separates the euros from the centimes: deux euros cinquante.
*Virgule* (comma) is how you read a decimal number in mathematics, not a price. In a café the waiter says deux euros cinquante.

activities.title: Listen: the numbers from 0 to 100
activities.text: Listen to each line, first slowly and then at normal speed, and repeat it aloud. The hints in italics are written with Finnish letters: capitals show the stressed syllable, and *õ*, *ã* and *ẽ* are nasal vowels. Watch the last five lines carefully: they are the surprise of French numbers.

activities.title: Watch: from 61 to 100
activities.text: Now listen to a second voice. Watch the chapters from 61 to 100 (about a minute and a half). Say each number aloud after the speaker. Write down the three numbers that you found hardest to hear or to say, and check them in the list above.

activities.title: Work out the numbers
activities.text: These numbers were not in the list. Work them out from their parts.

activities.title: What did you notice?
activities.prompt: How are the French numbers from 90 to 99 built?

choices.feedback: Yes: 90 is quatre-vingt-dix ($4 \cdot 20 + 10$), 93 is quatre-vingt-treize ($4 \cdot 20 + 13$), and so on up to quatre-vingt-dix-neuf.

choices.text: Nine tens plus a number from 0 to 9.
choices.feedback: That is how Finnish and English do it (*yhdeksänkymmentä*, *ninety*). In France, 90 is $4 \cdot 20 + 10$: quatre-vingt-dix.

choices.text: Sixty plus a number from 30 to 39.
choices.feedback: Sixty is the base of 60–79 only. From 80 the base is quatre-vingts ($4 \cdot 20$), and 90 is quatre-vingt-dix.

choices.text: A new word, as with 11 to 16.
choices.feedback: The words from 11 to 16 are new words, but 90–99 are built from parts: $4 \cdot 20 + 10$ … 19, quatre-vingt-dix … quatre-vingt-dix-neuf.

activities.title: Back to your predictions
activities.prompt: Compare your two predictions with the theory. Then answer the opening question in English in one or two sentences: why is 97 one of the hardest prices to catch in a French shop?

activities.title: Listen in pairs: what does it cost?
activities.text: Work in pairs with one device each. The French lines are hidden behind *Show the text*: the listener does not open them until after *Check*. **Partner A** plays the five lines of table A, one at a time (normal speed first, *Slowly* if B asks). **Partner B** does not look at A's screen and chooses the prices in the list under table A. Then swap: B plays table B, and A chooses in the list under it. (If a browser has no French voice, the text is shown and the partner reads the lines aloud instead.) Before you press *Check*, the listener may ask once: Vous pouvez répéter, s'il vous plaît ?

activities.title: Read the receipt
Asking about prices
Role-play: at the market
activities.text:
Work in pairs. **A** sells fruit at the market in Aix: write four fruits and a price for each on paper (between 0,50 € and 9,90 €) and do not show it. **B** buys two or three things: greet, ask the prices, ask for the total, check that you understood, pay and say goodbye. Then swap roles with new prices. Speak without reading if you can.

Word bank

Bonjour, madame / monsieur, les citrons (lemons), les abricots (apricots), les pêches (peaches), les tomates, un melon, le kilo, C'est combien ?, Ça fait combien ?, Vous pouvez répéter ?, Plus lentement, s'il vous plaît, Voilà, Merci, au revoir

Sentence starters

  • Bonjour, monsieur. Les citrons, c'est combien ?
  • Et le melon, c'est combien ?
  • Je voudrais un kilo d'abricots, s'il vous plaît.
  • Ça fait combien ?
  • Pardon, vous pouvez répéter, s'il vous plaît ?
  • Voilà. Merci, au revoir !

The seller: Bonjour ! Vous désirez ?, Le kilo de citrons, c'est trois euros quarante., Ça fait … euros …, Merci, bonne journée !

activities.title: Role-play: your dialogue
activities.prompt: After both rounds, write the dialogue of one round in French, at least six lines, with the prices in words. Write each price in digits too.
activities.pair: Perform the role-play with a partner first, then write it together.
activities.model: - A : Bonjour ! Vous désirez ? - B : Bonjour, madame. Les abricots, c'est combien ? - A : Quatre euros quatre-vingt-dix le kilo. (4,90 €) - B : Pardon, vous pouvez répéter, s'il vous plaît ? - A : Quatre euros… quatre-vingt-dix. - B : Je voudrais un kilo d'abricots et deux citrons, s'il vous plaît. Ça fait combien ? - A : Alors, les abricots, quatre euros quatre-vingt-dix, et les citrons, un euro vingt. Ça fait six euros dix. (4,90 € + 1,20 € = 6,10 €) - B : Voilà. Merci, au revoir ! - A : Merci, bonne journée !
criteria: **Communicates the message:** we greet, ask at least two prices and the total, pay and say goodbye.
**Numbers right:** every price in words matches the price in digits, and the total is correct.
**Polite and clear:** we use *vous*, *s'il vous plaît* and *merci*, and we ask for a repetition when we need it.
**Pronunciation understandable:** we link deux‿euros and similar pairs and do not pronounce the *t* in quatre-vingt-un.

activities.title: Extension: phone numbers
activities.text: French phone numbers have ten digits and are written in five pairs: 06 39 98 56 78. They are usually said in pairs too, so you need every number from 0 to 99. Numbers that start with 06 or 07 are mobile phones. Listen to the two numbers (they come from ranges that are never given to real phones), then dictate an invented number of your own to a partner, pair by pair, and check what they wrote.

activities.title: Extension: vowel combinations
activities.text: Many number words contain two vowels that make one sound: *trois* and *soixante* (*oi*), *deux* and *neuf* (*eu*), *douze* (*ou*), *treize* and *seize* (*ei*). Watch the video and note which combinations it shows and how each one sounds. Then find one number word for each combination you noted, and say it to your partner.

activities.title: 1. A price by ear
activities.prompt: In a souvenir shop in Aix-en-Provence, you hear: « Ça fait quatre-vingt-dix-sept euros. » How much do you pay?

choices.feedback: Yes: quatre-vingt is $4 \cdot 20$ = 80, and dix-sept is 17. $80 + 17 = 97$.
You heard 80 and 7, but dix-sept at the end is 17, not 7: $80 + 17 = 97$ €.
77 is soixante-dix-sept ($60 + 17$). Quatre-vingt-dix-sept starts with $4 \cdot 20 = 80$: 97 €.
Quatre-vingt is one part of the number, 4 · 20, not four euros. The price is $80 + 17 = 97$ €.

activities.title: 2. Writing a price the French way
activities.prompt: You write a price list for the café in French. How do you write two euros eighty?

choices.feedback: Yes: a decimal comma, and the euro sign after the number with a space.
This is how English writes it. French uses a decimal comma and puts the euro sign after the number: 2,80 €.
The euro sign is in the right place, but French uses a decimal comma, not a point: 2,80 €.
The decimal comma is right, but in French the euro sign comes after the number: 2,80 €.

activities.title: 3. Linking before a vowel
activities.prompt: How do you pronounce six euros?

choices.feedback: Yes. *Euros* starts with a vowel, so the final *x* of *six* is linked to it, and in liaison it sounds like *z*.
*Six* has a sharp *s* only when it stands alone. Before a vowel it is linked with a *z*: *si-zö-RO*.
People will understand you, but French links the two words: the silent *x* becomes a *z* before the vowel. Say *si-zö-RO*.
This is the Finnish habit of saying every letter. The final *s* of *euros* is silent, *eu* is close to *ö*, and *six* is linked: *si-zö-RO*.

activities.title: 4. Write: what did it cost?
activities.prompt: After the visit you send a French text message to a friend: what you bought at a café in Aix, the price of each thing in words, and the total. Write three to five sentences.
activities.model: Salut ! Au café, à Aix, je prends un jus d'orange et un sandwich. Le jus d'orange coûte trois euros soixante-dix (3,70 €) et le sandwich quatre euros quatre-vingt-quinze (4,95 €). Ça fait huit euros soixante-cinq (8,65 €). C'est cher, mais c'est bon ! À bientôt !
criteria: I name at least two things and give the price of each in words.
Every price in words matches the digits, with the French decimal comma.
The total is correct and said with *Ça fait …*.
I use the right forms for 70–99 (*soixante-dix*, *quatre-vingts*, *quatre-vingt-dix*).
